record.paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
record.context_brief: Cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow
record.original_question: What is the cosmological origin of the universal thermodynamic arrow of time? In particular, should the present arrow be explained by a special low-entropy condition at the big bang, by a Boltzmann-style giant fluctuation in an eternal universe, or by some other mechanism; and if the low-entropy condition is tied to the big bang, how can one understand the consequences for oscillating-universe models, where the thermodynamic arrow would otherwise have to reverse direction?

evidence.quote: Its origin has, therefore, usually been discussed in a cosmological context. For example, one may assume a special cosmic initial condition at the big bang.

Boltzmann’s proposal seems to imply, though, that it would then be far more probable if the present state of the universe – including all memories – had just formed in a chance fluctuation, since this state would still possess very low, but much higher entropy than the extremely improbable state in the distant past.

If, on the other hand, the low entropy is related to the special conditions at the big bang, the thermodynamical time arrow would have to change direction in an oscillating universe, while opposite arrows in causally connected parts of the universe seem to be excluded for dynamical reasons.

artifact.category_tag: arrow of time and cosmological initial conditions
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a universe modeled by a time-symmetric fundamental dynamics (for instance, a Hamiltonian or unitary evolution on a phase space or Hilbert space) together with a coarse-graining that defines a Boltzmann-type entropy S(t). Empirically, S(t) is observed to increase monotonically in one temporal direction, defining a universal thermodynamic arrow of time.

Provide a cosmological account of the origin of this arrow by addressing the following:

(a) Determine whether the observed monotonic increase of S(t) can be explained by postulating a special low-entropy boundary condition at the big bang (a "past hypothesis"), and formulate precisely what such a condition must require of the initial macrostate so that typical microstates compatible with it evolve toward higher-entropy macrostates.

(b) Evaluate the alternative hypothesis, due to Boltzmann, that the universe is eternal and in global thermal equilibrium, and that the present low-entropy state is a giant statistical fluctuation. Show, using the relative measures of fluctuations of given size in an equilibrium ensemble, whether or not this hypothesis is consistent with the observation that the present state of the universe is not the smallest fluctuation compatible with current memories and records (the "Boltzmann brain" / typicality problem).

(c) Assuming the low-entropy condition is attached to the big bang, analyze the consequences for a recollapsing or oscillating cosmological model. In particular, decide whether the thermodynamic arrow must reverse during the contracting phase, and reconcile this with the dynamical requirement that causally connected regions of the universe cannot simultaneously support oppositely directed thermodynamic arrows.

(d) If neither (a) nor (b) is satisfactory, propose an alternative mechanism (for example, based on quantum cosmology, decoherence, or a dynamical selection principle) that derives the universal thermodynamic arrow from the underlying time-symmetric laws together with cosmological structure, and verify its compatibility with the constraints in (c).
artifact.status_search_result: The cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow of time remains an open foundational problem. Recent reviews and research (e.g., works by Carroll, Wallace, Goldstein–Tumulka, Albert, and others through the 2020s) continue to debate the past hypothesis, Boltzmann-fluctuation scenarios (now pressured by the Boltzmann-brain problem), and quantum-cosmological alternatives, with no consensus resolution.

status_evidence.title: The Cosmological Origins of Time Asymmetry
status_evidence.snippet: The question of why the universe began in a low-entropy state, and whether this 'past hypothesis' suffices to explain the thermodynamic arrow, remains contested.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is treated as still open in current foundations-of-physics literature.

status_evidence.title: From Eternity to Here: The Quest for the Ultimate Theory of Time (Carroll)
status_evidence.snippet: Carroll and collaborators argue the low-entropy past is not yet explained by known dynamics; Boltzmann-brain considerations rule out simple fluctuation accounts.
status_evidence.claim: Mainstream cosmology regards the origin of the arrow as unresolved.
